rationale: On AgentHarm harmfulness judgments (N=97) hosted Jev reached 84.54% accuracy with ECE 0.068, against 61.86-85.57% accuracy and ECE 0.089-0.349 for the nine generative configurations: level with thinking Qwen3.8-27B (84.54%) and one point below thinking GLM-5.3-Flash (85.57%). This is a single sub-benchmark, run once, with no intervals (App. D.6, Tables 25-27).

On the 10,938 JEVal choice/noul questions Jev's ECE was 0.0532, lower than every generative configuration (0.0784 for thinking GLM-5.3-Flash to 0.2526; GPT-6-Luna 0.1159), at 78.38% accuracy (Table 1). But on 100-item tasks with analytically known distributions it put 89.35% of the mass on the true mode against 35.60% true (E_mode 53.75 pp prior, 28.12 pp posterior), the largest probability errors of all configurations evaluated (Table 2, Fig. 5, Sec. 5.1).

Jev predicted 277,500 SocioBench respondent-question pairs at 37.69% accuracy, against 37.90% for non-thinking DeepSeek-V4-Flash, at 0.50 s vs 174.0 s per item (Table 5). It agreed less with a reference interest profiler (Jaccard 53.88% vs 65.24-65.86%; Table 4). The authors' InnerJev-27B voter agents called 47/51 states vs 46/51 for GPT-4o-mini agents, but with about twice the vote-share error (MAE 6.52 vs 3.06 pp) and a Democratic bias of +3.73 vs +2.31; two preliminary hosted-Jev runs also overestimated Harris (Sec. 5.4.3, Table 40).

As a zero-shot Noul detector, hosted Jev reached ROC-AUC 0.95-1.0 on all eight benchmarks (prompt injection, jailbreak input, harmful content, AI-generated text), with 87-99% accuracy on the six security benchmarks at a threshold fitted on 20-100 held-out calibration examples. On AI-text detection the default 0.5 threshold gave 78% mean accuracy, which rose to 89% only with the fitted threshold. Open NanoJev was near or below ROC-AUC 0.5 on three of the four tasks (Sec. V-B, Table VI, Fig. 8).

On 200 GPT-4o-generated states per task, a Jev-specific injection reached 100%/100%/97.2% ASR against hosted Jev and a universal suffix 100%/100%/97.0% (clean accuracy 100%); each template attack reached 88.5-100% on at least one task. Poisoning 5-10% of training data implanted backdoors in NanoJev with 76.1-100% target ASR while clean accuracy stayed at 90.4-94.0%. Conditional instructions in user input made hosted Jev reveal hidden gender, age group, heart-disease and ethnicity attributes with 100% coverage and accuracy (Tables I, II, V).

In deployment, hosted Jev's labels alone leaked all four tested private attributes (100% coverage and accepted accuracy on 200 states each), and repeated interval queries recovered 10 privacy-related facts that GPT-6 declined to give directly. Jev also served as an oracle that raised the judged harmfulness of 100 harmful plans from 2.3 to 4.5 (100% success), and 200 of its labels trained a NanoJev surrogate from 49% to 92% agreement; NanoJev membership inference reached a mean ROC-AUC of 0.64 (Tables III, V, Sec. IV-A4, App. C).

In-distribution, the authors' SearchJev cut mean ECE by 74.4% and 40.7% relative to same-size Qwen3.5 AR (JSON) models, and hosted Jev 1.13 kept the lowest mean ECE; on evidence sufficiency SearchJev-4B reached 96.0% accuracy vs 79.8% for Jev and 57.7% for Qwen3.5-4B AR (Table 3). On held-out datasets calibration did not transfer: SearchJev-4B's ECE was 26.9 on rewriting and 15.4 on verification, against 24.1 and 3.7 for Qwen3.5-4B AR and 5.6 and 3.7 for Jev, whose routing ECE was 20.0 (Table 5, Sec. 5.3).

On 100 BrowseComp-Plus questions run once, dual-system agents that accept confident SearchJev decisions and delegate the rest to Qwen3.5-27B reached 46.0% (0.8B) and 54.0% (4B) accuracy, against 45.0% for the System-2-only agent and 46.0% with Jev 1.13 in the System-1 slot. Median active time was 868-1102 s vs 4080 s. However, the gate threshold cannot be recovered from the logs and no explicit System-2 short-decision calls were recorded, so the contribution of escalation is unverified (Tables 4 and 8, App. D.3).

Given a reject/escalate option, Jev requested new candidates for 45/48 contracts that had no valid candidate (generative LLMs 1-16/48). It escalated only 4/120 forwarding instances with no feasible path (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 67, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite 49, GLM-4.7-Flash 109, Qwen3.5-4B 2/120). It chose the correct placement action in 50/120 current-conflict and 11/120 resolved-conflict observation cases (Tables X and XI, Sec. VII-C).

Moving feasibility checks out of the engine into a public gate raised Jev's placement correctness from 29/120 to 84/120 (+45.8 pp [37.5, 54.2]), the highest of five engines (52-71/120). Gains were smaller with shared quotas (14 to 42/120, below GLM-4.7-Flash's 50) and with fault-domain separation (6 to 45/120, below Gemini's 61), against 120/120 for a full deterministic rule. The intervention also changes instructions and refresh; only 9/139 surveyed families distinguish format, task and outcome gates (Tables III, XII, XX).

Asking 27,367 Study 1 survey pairs in both orders flipped the winner in 8.8% of pairs (8.5% in Study 2), with a pull toward the second slot of -0.0358. Flips concentrated where confidence was low: 36.55% below p=.50 and 0.00% above .95. Forward and reversed scales correlated 0.982, and weak stochastic transitivity held in 98.37% of triples (App. B, Table 3).

Asked once per question, Jev had lower ECE than GPT-6 Luna's token probabilities on all eight human-labelled reading tasks (e.g. V-Dem 0.057 vs 0.390, difference 0.333 [0.318, 0.347]) and higher AUROC on seven of eight. But Qwen3.8-27B was better calibrated on the four pairwise tasks (survey pairs 0.049 vs 0.109, difference -0.060 [-0.091, -0.009]), and the gap to Luna disappeared when probabilities were averaged over both presentation orders (Fig. 2, Tables 9-10, App. B).

Across seven political-science replications scored against human benchmarks, Jev matched or approached GPT-6 Luna and Qwen3.8-27B. It was worse on 2023 tweet relevance (76.2% vs 84.2%) and sentiment (rho 0.740 vs 0.816/0.841) and better on V-Dem (0.68 vs 0.63/0.59) and attack type. It took 0.09-0.27 s per decision vs 0.75-1.04 s for Luna, but was not cheaper than Luna at batch prices (Luna cheaper on 6 of 7 tasks). Its architecture, base model and training data are undisclosed (Tables 1-2, 9-10, App. E).

On HakemBench's Turkish guardrail track the released model caught 194/217 prompt-injection attacks but passed only 128/201 harmless look-alikes; on moderation it caught 150/157 offensive and passed 186/196 clean messages. The author flags these numbers as shaped by reading earlier test results and possibly inflated by style likeness. Its overall decision quality (macro F1 0.705) is below Jev 1.13 (0.851) and below every generative model on the board (0.741-0.901) (Secs. 4 and 6, Table 2).

The order-invariant head makes order sensitivity 0.000 by construction (verified bit for bit by a permutation test). A sequential head trained with shuffled options changed 2.3-2.8% of answers under reordering at similar accuracy. Paraphrase agreement was 0.883 [0.833, 0.932] vs 0.926 [0.889, 0.963] for Jev 1.13, with overlapping intervals (Secs. 2 and 6, Table 4).

Temperature scaling lowered smooth ECE on the support development set (0.050 to 0.038) but raised it on held-out support questions (0.027 to 0.045 for Run 1, which never trained on them). The guardrail track had smooth ECE 0.158 vs 0.025-0.084 on other tracks, and the 'not sure' signal let 18 wrong answers through out of 148 guardrail answers at confidence >=0.99 (0.122 [0.078, 0.184]). The board calibration axis was 0.482, below Jev 1.13 (0.706), GLM 5.3 (0.706), GPT-5.6 Sol (0.727) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (0.806) but above DeepSeek V4 Pro (0.386) and Qwen3.5-4B (0.438) (Sec. 5, Tables 1-2).
